passages.title: The Goosenecks of the San Juan River
passages.content:
The San Juan River is in southern Utah. Long ago, it flowed across a flat plain. The river took a long, winding path. Then geologic forces pushed the Colorado Plateau upward. Some experts think this made the river flow faster. The water cut deeper into old rock.

Today, the river makes big bends called goosenecks. In Goosenecks State Park, the river runs through a canyon 1,000 feet (300 meters) deep. In some places, it nearly loops back on itself. One part is very curvy. The river travels 5.5 miles between two points that are only 1.3 miles apart.

At night, the park has very dark skies. Its remote, high-desert location and 360-degree views helped it become an International Dark Sky Park in 2021.

passages.title: Hubble Looks at a Very Old Star Cluster
passages.content:
This NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image shows Messier 30, or M30. It is a globular cluster. That is a roughly spherical group of stars. It can have from tens of thousands to millions of stars. M30 lies about 27,500 light-years away in the constellation Capricornus. It is named after Charles Messier, a French astronomer.

Globular clusters are very old. Astronomers estimate their ages are between 11.5 and 13.5 billion years. Our Milky Way galaxy has at least 150 globular clusters. They orbit in a huge, diffuse region called the halo. Because they are ancient, they can give us clues about how our galaxy developed long ago.

M30 and many other globular clusters orbit in the opposite direction from the way our galaxy spins. This may mean they did not form in our galaxy. Our Milky Way may have captured them in the distant past. Hubble has observed M30 multiple times.

passages.title: The Island of Cyprus
passages.content:
Cyprus is an island in the Mediterranean Sea. It began to form about 90 million years ago. Hot rock came up from the seafloor and became hard rock. Later, forces inside the Earth pushed this rock up. The rock is called ophiolite. It is green and looks like snake skin. You can still see it in the Troodos Mountains.

Over time, the island changed. Rivers carried sand and mud into the sea. This made two land bridges. They joined two smaller islands into one big island. The southern part is now called the Akrotiri Peninsula. It has a salt lake. In winter, the lake fills with water. In summer, it dries out. Flamingos come to the lake to eat tiny shrimp. The shrimp have pink color in them. This makes the flamingos pink.

Cyprus is also famous for cats and snakes. Long ago, there were many snakes. People say a queen sent cats from Egypt to catch the snakes. Today, there are more than one million cats on the island. That is about the same as the number of people.

passages.title: City Lights Before Dawn
passages.content:
On October 18, 2026, the sky was clear over much of the eastern United States before dawn. An astronaut aboard the International Space Station took a wide-angle photo at 4:54 a.m. Central Daylight Time. The photo shows bright city lights on a dark landscape. Chicago and Detroit are among the brightest areas. Indianapolis, Cincinnati, Louisville, and highways also shine.

To the left, a green and orange band appears above the lights. This band of light is airglow, produced when sunlight strikes atoms and molecules in the upper atmosphere. To the right, sunlight comes over the horizon. Sunrise was about one hour away on the East Coast and about two hours away in Chicago.

The photo shows city lights and airglow, and such nighttime photos help scientists study changes on Earth. Scientists can use these photos to track changes in cities and lighting over time.

During the call, students will see the space station in real time. They will learn how everyday activities change in microgravity. The event also starts a new NASA and ClassCrunchLabs Foundation collaboration. They want to broaden access to STEM learning for students.

passages.title: Chip Resistor Cracks on Printed Circuit Boards
passages.content:
Chip resistors are used in many NASA projects. Cracks in their ceramic bodies are rare. But two cracked chip resistors were found during environmental testing. Both failures happened during thermal cycling after vibration testing. The two resistors were near the edge of two identical boards. The cracks went across the short axis. Experts concluded that bending caused the cracks. They did not find a defective resistor lot or fatigue.

Possible causes included board bending, the resistors' position, too much solder, and mounting stress. Too much solder on top can make a rigid joint and pass board bending into the ceramic.

NASA recommends careful placement, controlled solder, checking solder joints, and thermal shock tests to reduce cracking risks in ceramic components on printed circuit boards.

passages.title: Storms Over the Pacific
passages.content:
In 2026, the Northwest Pacific had a busy storm season. It started in April. A storm named Sinlaku became very strong. It hit Micronesia, Guam, and the Northern Mariana Islands. After that, many more named storms formed. By late October, the ocean was still full of storms.

A satellite took a picture on October 29, 2026. It showed Super Typhoon In-fa near the Mariana Islands. In-fa was the fifth typhoon to affect the Mariana Islands that year. It had a big, round eye and a nearly circular shape. Scientists call these "annular" storms, or "doughnuts." Annular storms are rare. They are only about 4 percent of tropical cyclones in this area.

At the same time, the remnants of Typhoon Champi moved toward Alaska. Champi had been a very strong storm. It brought strong winds and heavy rain to Taiwan, Guam, parts of China, and Japan. When its remnants reached Alaska, some areas had high winds and heavy rain and snow.

passages.title: The Hammer Test: What NASA Measures
passages.content:
NASA uses a hammer test to study how structures move and shake. An instrumented hammer hits the structure. It measures the force. The test does not need a perfect, smooth force shape. The force can have small ripples or even separate contacts. The full force and the structure's response are both measured.

When the structure has no force on it, it keeps vibrating for a short time. Then it may be hit again. The new hit acts on that vibration. The force shape changes how the structure is excited. But the shape does not make the record invalid. What matters is accurate measurement and good signal quality.

NASA says a test is good only if the measurements can answer the test's goal. So a smooth-looking force alone does not prove a test is good. Each hammer test must be judged by its purpose and by accurate, complete force and response measurements over the needed range.

passages.title: November Skywatching
passages.content:
November has many things to see in the night sky. Around November 5, the Southern Taurids meteor shower peaks. Around November 12, the Northern Taurids peak. Each shower makes about five meteors per hour under ideal conditions. Sometimes a bright fireball can appear.

The Leonids are best before dawn on November 17 and 18, after the Moon sets. Under ideal conditions, they may make around 15 meteors per hour. To watch, find a dark place and give your eyes about half an hour to adjust.

On the mornings of November 15 and 16, look southeast before sunrise. Mars and Jupiter appear about 1.2 degrees apart. Jupiter is the brighter point of light, with reddish Mars nearby. On November 24, a full supermoon rises. It is the first of three supermoons in a row.

passages.title: Pennsylvania’s Grand Canyon
passages.content:
North-central Pennsylvania has a famous gorge. It is called Pine Creek Gorge. People also call it the “Grand Canyon of Pennsylvania.” The gorge is about 45 miles (72 kilometers) long. It is about 1,500 feet (460 meters) deep in its deepest place.

The gorge does not have steep desert rock walls. Instead, green plants cover its slopes. In autumn, the leaves turn red and gold. Many visitors come to see these colors. Glaciers helped make the gorge, but ice did not carve it. Long ago, Pine Creek flowed north. Then glaciers blocked the river. Later, water flowed south and shaped the valley.

Today, forests cover the hills around the gorge. Black bears and many songbirds live there. In 1968, the area became a National Natural Landmark.

passages.content:
In 1977, NASA launched two spacecraft called Voyager 1 and Voyager 2. They visited the four largest planets: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. The spacecraft used the gravity of each planet to move on to the next one. This was a big tour of our solar system.

Each Voyager carries a Golden Record. It has spoken greetings in 55 languages, 27 music tracks, and 116 images. The record also has sounds from Earth. It is protected by a metal cover.

Voyager 1 is very far away. On November 18, 2026, it will be one light-day from the Sun. That is 16.1 billion miles. A light-day is a measure of distance, not time. Both Voyagers still send science back to Earth.

passages.title: Vega Island: The Ice Skull
passages.content:
Vega Island is in the cold Weddell Sea near Antarctica. Ice, rock, and glacial moraines on the island make a shape like a smiling skull. A rock outcrop looks like an eye socket. A lateral moraine looks like a mouth. A glacier forms the jawbone. The skull looks toward Devil Island.

NASA took pictures of Vega Island in March 2025 and October 2026. In March, snow covered the ice. In October, large areas had no snow. Darker ice was visible. Scientists said winter 2026 was warm. Less new snow fell, and wind and sublimation removed snow. Bare ice is darker than snow, so it absorbs more sunlight. This can make melting faster.

Scientists have studied Vega Island's ice for many years. They found 29 glaciers on the island. Since 1998, one glacier, Devil's Bay Glacier, has lost mass. Long ago, in 1901–1903, a Swedish expedition explored the area. Their ship was lost in pack ice. Two groups met at Cape Well-met, near the skull's forehead. Later, an Argentinean expedition rescued the survivors.

The book is more than facts. It also tells who is doing the work and where. So companies can find partners. It is not a story about the future. It shows what is real now and where space work is going next.

passages.title: A New NASA Challenge for Safer Medicine

NASA and the NIH have a new challenge. It is called QuSAFE. The goal is to make medicine safer. The challenge uses tiny lab models. These models are like small parts of the human body. They can help scientists test drugs without using many animals.

Today, some tests are not strong enough. They are noisy. They can miss weak or early signals. Some tests also hurt the models, so scientists cannot watch them for a long time. New sensing tools can be much more sensitive. They can find very small signals. This helps scientists see changes over time.

The QuSAFE Challenge offers up to $7.1 million in prizes. Submissions open on December 15, 2026. They close on July 27, 2027. This work can help science in space and on Earth.

passages.title: A Very Old Rock from Mars
passages.content:
This is a slice of a rock called Teghaza 001. It is one of the most ancient Martian meteorites ever found on Earth. Scientists used this slice to find out how old the rock is. They looked at it with reflected light. The light helped them find minerals in the rock.

Some parts of the slice are brighter. They are iron-titanium oxides. Some parts are medium gray. They are pyroxene. These minerals tell a story about how Mars' crust and mantle formed. Other parts are darker gray. They are shocked plagioclase. Extreme pressure during impacts made them that way. One impact sent this rock through space to Earth.

The slice also has fine grain carbonate, sulfate and clay minerals. These formed on Earth after the rock arrived.

NASA's Curiosity rover is on Mars. It is getting ready to drill at a new place called "Nazca." The rover moved to a spot near a rock called "Chiu Chiu." Chiu Chiu was not good for drilling. That is like salt crystals you can grow in your kitchen.

The team will use the rover's arm and cameras to study the shapes closely. They will take many pictures to make 3D models. They will also use a laser to learn what the rock is made of, even deeper inside. All this work happens before the drill test. Curiosity also took pictures of Mars' moon Phobos at night. passages.title: The Land of the Standing-Up Rocks
passages.content:
Long ago, a volcano erupted in Arizona. It sent ash and rock across the land. Later, the ground above the empty magma chamber fell down. This made a big, deep hole. Over time, wind and water slowly cut the hard rock into tall spires and canyons. The Apache people called the area "The Land of the Standing-Up Rocks."

Many rock pinnacles stand hundreds of feet tall. Some large boulders sit on top of other rocks. In 1924, people made the area a national monument to keep its special rocks safe. In October 2026, it became Chiricahua National Park.

The park has four different natural regions. Many kinds of plants grow there, including cacti, pines, and oaks. The park is also one of Arizona's "sky islands." These are mountain ranges that rise up from the desert around them.

It seemed to bump along the edge of the island's underwater shelf. South Georgia has slowed or stopped icebergs before. In 2025, Iceberg A-23A ran aground there and later broke apart. A-81 moved a long way, but near South Georgia it moved slowly.

passages.title: Red Leaves Seen From Space
passages.content:
In fall, leaves change color. They lose green chlorophyll. Then red and orange colors can show. NASA uses a satellite called PACE to watch this from space. PACE looks at Earth every day. It measures red, orange, yellow, and green in forests.

Maps from September 29 to October 4 show strong red colors in Alaska, northern Canada, Mongolia, and Russia. From October 5 to 11, the red colors moved south. More red appeared in China, Mongolia, and the Mid-Atlantic.

Scientists need to study Tinga more to understand the rocks. Tinga tells a story about exciting events near Jezero crater. The rover will keep exploring and sharing Mars's history.

passages.title: El Niño: Warm Water in the Pacific
passages.content:
El Niño is a natural climate pattern. It happens about every two to seven years. It brings warmer-than-normal water to parts of the equatorial Pacific Ocean.

Every El Niño grows from a feedback loop between the atmosphere and the ocean. Trade winds normally keep warm water in the western Pacific. When those winds weaken, the warm water moves east. Satellites can measure the height of the sea surface. Water expands as it warms, so higher sea levels in the central and eastern Pacific show the heat of El Niño.

In October 2026, sea levels were higher than normal in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. This pattern looked like October 1997, during another very strong El Niño. But each El Niño is different, and scientists say it is hard to find a “typical” one.

passages.title: A Giant Lens in Space
passages.content: A galaxy is very far away. Its gravity can bend light from a galaxy behind it. This is called gravitational lensing. It works like a giant lens in space. The light bends and makes the far galaxy look bigger. In one Hubble image, a closer galaxy is about 4.5 billion light-years away. The farther galaxy is about 8 billion light-years away. The far galaxy appears as two arcs, one large and one small. This is called an arc-counterarc pair. The closer galaxy's mass bends the light. More mass means a stronger lens. Scientists study this bending to learn about dark matter. Dark matter is invisible. It makes up most of the mass in the universe. The visible matter is not enough to explain the bending. Hubble takes sharp pictures of these lenses one at a time. The new Roman Space Telescope will see a much larger area of the sky. Then it can find many more lenses.

passages.title: Perseverance Sets a Driving Record on Mars
passages.content:
The Perseverance rover drives on Mars. On Sol 2006, its odometer reached 45.22 kilometers (28.10 miles). This set a new record for the farthest distance driven on another celestial body. Its engineering twin on Earth even received a plaque from Guinness World Records.

Two months before, the rover was about 200 meters away from the milestone. But it was in a very scientifically interesting area. So it spent time making short drives to study ancient rocks. When it was finally ready to move on, it drove past the record.

The rover also faced hard terrain, such as dense boulder fields and steep slopes. The team ran thousands of simulations. They raised the rover's tilt limit to 24 degrees. They also updated the rover's braking software to avoid rock hazards. The team is using these lessons to reinvent how the rover drives on Mars.

passages.title: NASA's Quiet Rooms for Testing Aircraft Noise
passages.content:
NASA has special rooms to test airplane noise. One room is a big dome. It is called the Aero-Acoustic Propulsion Laboratory. The dome has 17,000 thick fiberglass wedges on the walls and floor. These wedges absorb sound. So there are no echoes inside. When the dome was built in 1993, it was the first free-standing dome of its kind to reduce sound.

Inside the dome, NASA tests small models of aircraft engines. One test rig is the Small Hot Jet Acoustic Rig. It tests nozzles up to 5 cm wide. Another is the Nozzle Acoustic Test Rig. It checks noise reduction ideas before full-size engine tests. The dome also houses the DGEN Aero-propulsion Research Turbofan.

NASA uses these rooms to learn how to make airplanes quieter. Quieter planes help people who live near airports.

passages.title: Measuring Sound and Air at NASA
passages.content:
NASA teams study airflow and sound. They use special tools. One tool is a rotating microphone rake. It spins and listens to engine noise. A normal microphone cannot measure some tones. Engineers at NASA Glenn started using rotating microphones in the 1990s. They use them in wind tunnels and on real engines.

NASA also uses microphone phased arrays. These place many microphones in 1D, 2D, or 3D groups. When the sound data is processed, teams can find where noise comes from. NASA Glenn has an Array48 system. It helps locate noise in model jets, a rotor fan model, and a full-scale F404 engine.

Other tools measure air speed. Hot wire probes and laser Doppler velocimeters measure air before, after, and between engine parts. The data help teams find noise sources. They also check computer programs that predict engine noise.

passages.title: NASA Software Helps Predict Aircraft Noise
passages.content:
NASA researchers at Glenn work on software to predict noise from aircraft engines. This software helps engineers design and study new and better aircraft engines. People can ask NASA for copies of the software.

One program is called JeNo. It predicts jet noise. JeNo can give answers faster than some other methods. It works for some simple jets. Another program is called MGBK. Researchers used MGBK to study chevrons. Chevrons are small serrations on the edge of a nozzle. They can help reduce noise. Today, many commercial aircraft engines have chevrons.

passages.title: NASA Engineers Use Computer Software to Study Shaking Rockets
passages.content:
Rockets shake and vibrate strongly when they go up into space. Spacecraft carry delicate science tools. NASA engineers must predict how these forces affect every part of a spacecraft before launch. Engineers at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida use a computer software tool. This tool helps them study shock and vibration. It also helps them make sure rockets and spacecraft can handle strong forces. This work makes missions safer.

Engineers used the software for the first time to check a company's rocket for a NASA mission. The company did vibration testing but not shock testing. NASA engineers used a template to run what-if comparisons and see how the structure behaves. The software helps find weak spots early, before hardware is built. It has saved months of work.

Rockets are designed to absorb shocks and vibrations. But these forces can cause wear and tear or even flight failures. Engineers define how strong the vibration and shock levels are. Then they check that all parts are tested to those levels. Once a rocket leaves the launch pad, most problems cannot be fixed. So early identification is very important.

passages.content:
Four people in NASA's CHAPEA Mission 2 just spent one year in a simulated Mars home. The home is at NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston. The crew entered the 1,700 square foot 3D-printed habitat on October 19, 2025. For 365 days, they lived and worked as if they were on Mars. They grew crops, managed limited resources, and practiced spacewalks on a simulated Martian surface.

The crew members are Ross Elder, Ellen Ellis, Matthew Montgomery, and James Spicer. Each person had a special job, like commander or medical officer. During the mission, they could only talk with their families by email. Messages had a Mars-like delay. They will exit the habitat on October 31. After that, they will spend two weeks with NASA scientists. The scientists will study the crew's health and performance data. This data can help NASA plan for future long missions to Mars.

passages.title: Autumn Colors in Poland's Mountains
passages.content:
Autumn brings big changes to the Bieszczady Mountains in southern Poland. The air grows cooler, and the days get shorter. Brown bears walk through the Carpathian Mountains. They eat a lot to get ready for winter sleep. Another sign of autumn is the trees. Beech trees and other deciduous trees turn red and gold.

In October 2026, a NASA satellite took a picture of this area. The picture shows Bieszczady National Park. European beech trees are the main trees in the forest. Cooler air and less daylight stop the trees from making chlorophyll. This green stuff usually makes leaves green. When it fades, yellow and red colors show.

Beech forests in this area grow only up to about 1,000 to 1,260 meters high. Above that, there are open meadows called polonina. These meadows have grasses and small bushes. They look tan in autumn because they lose their summer green. The park is also home to European bison, brown bears, and lynx.

passages.title: Hubble Looks at a Spiral Galaxy from the Side
passages.content:
The NASA Hubble Space Telescope took a picture of a spiral galaxy. The galaxy is named NGC 1827. It is about 37 million light-years away from Earth. It is in the constellation Columba, the Dove. In the picture, we see the galaxy from its edge. This is called an edge-on view.

The picture shows bright-blue parts along the galaxy's disk. Dark dust lanes are also in the disk. New stars are likely forming there. A bright star appears just to the left of the galaxy's bright center. But this star is not part of the galaxy. It is between us and the galaxy.

Hubble took this picture for a survey. The survey looks at 260 small satellite galaxies around 22 big galaxies like our Milky Way. Hubble has already observed 111 of these small galaxies. The data will help us learn more about small galaxies.

passages.title: When the Lights Went Out After Hurricane Isaias
passages.content:
Hurricane Isaias brought heavy rain and strong winds to the Gulf Coast. The storm hit near Destin, Florida, on the evening of October 9, 2026. Winds knocked down trees and power lines, so many people lost power.

NASA satellites take pictures of city lights at night. The images showed Pensacola and Destin were much darker after the storm. There were also dark gaps along the road between the two cities. These dark areas suggest many homes and businesses had no power.

A few days later, the lights came back. By October 14, the light patterns looked like the time before the storm. NASA's pictures help workers see where help is still needed.

passages.title: NASA Watches a Very Strong El Niño
passages.content:
El Niño is a natural climate pattern. It happens every two to seven years. During El Niño, water in parts of the Pacific Ocean becomes warmer than normal. NASA uses satellites to watch it closely.

In January 2026, satellites saw a large, slow-moving pulse of warm water called a Kelvin wave. It moved heat from west to east across the Pacific. This warm water made sea levels rise in the eastern Pacific. In some places, the water rose by 30 to 40 centimeters.

El Niño can change weather around the world. Warm ocean water puts heat and moisture into the air. This can change rain patterns. El Niño can also make ocean water look more blue, because there is less phytoplankton, a tiny plant in the sea. NASA will keep watching with its satellites.

passages.title: Talking to Astronauts from Space
passages.content: Students in Florida will talk with NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney. The astronauts are on the International Space Station. They will answer questions from students. The questions are about STEM. STEM means science, technology, engineering, and math. The call starts at 12:30 p.m. EDT on Friday, Oct. 16. People can watch it online on the Learn With NASA YouTube channel. Sally Ride Elementary School in Orlando, Florida, hosts the event. Students in grades K-12 and the community can join. The event helps people learn more about space and STEM jobs. For over 25 years, people have lived and worked on the space station. They do science there. The space station helps NASA learn about human spaceflight. It also helps NASA prepare for future missions to the Moon and Mars.

passages.title: The Treble Clef in Space
passages.content:
Astronomers used NASA's Chandra telescope to study a strange shape in space. People call it the Treble Clef because it looks like a music sign. It is made of radio waves.

The Treble Clef sits inside two galaxy clusters. Galaxy clusters are some of the largest things in the universe. They hold hundreds of galaxies and huge clouds of hot gas. The hot gas is millions of degrees hot. Chandra found this gas, so we know a galaxy cluster is there.

The scientists think the Treble Clef formed in two steps. First, a supermassive black hole pushed out clouds of charged particles. This made bright radio waves. Later, the two clusters crashed together. The crash squeezed the cloud, and the radio waves got bright again. The shape itself is just pareidolia. That means people see a familiar shape, but there is no real link to music.

passages.title: A Moon Lander Gets Ready
passages.content:
A company called Voyager Technologies made a space lander. Its name is Griffin-1. The lander will go to the Moon later this year. It will carry more than 1,100 pounds of cargo. The cargo will go to Nobile Crater near the Moon's South Pole.

Before launch, Griffin-1 had many tests at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. The tests were like a real space trip. The lander felt hot and cold temperatures. It shook hard like during launch. It also heard a very loud sound, up to 153 decibels. The tests showed the lander is ready for space.

After the tests, Griffin-1 went back to Voyager's facility for final assembly. Soon it will get ready for launch.

passages.title: When Two Modes Meet
passages.content:
Structures can vibrate in different ways. These ways are called modes. Two modes may be close in frequency. Frequency is how fast a mode moves. When two modes are close, they can affect each other. Damping, which slows vibration, can connect them. This connection can change their shapes.

At first, the two frequencies move closer. The mode shapes become more complex. At a critical point, the two frequencies become equal. After that, the frequencies stay about the same. But their decay rates separate. Decay rate means how fast a vibration slows down.

If the connection is very strong, the mode shapes become simple again. But they are different from before. This helps us understand how two close modes interact.

passages.title: The Spider Crater in Australia
passages.content:
Spider Crater is in Western Australia. It has a funny name. From above, it looks a little like a big spider. It is not a real spider. It is a large hole made long ago when a space rock hit Earth. A NASA satellite took a picture of it on September 20, 2026.

The whole crater is about 13 kilometers by 11 kilometers. The middle part looks like a spider and is about 4 kilometers across. Its light-colored "legs" are hard rock. The other rock around it wore away over time. Long ago, some scientists were not sure how the crater formed. Later, geologists found signs of a space rock impact in the rocks. They also studied tiny bits of rock in the lab.

Scientists are not sure when the space rock hit. They think it was between about 900 million and 600 million years ago.

passages.title: Griffin-1 Gets Ready for the Moon
passages.content:
A lunar lander called Griffin-1 finished almost three months of testing at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. The tests show the spacecraft is ready for the hard conditions of launch, the trip to the Moon, and landing on the surface. Its last test was in a large chamber that is listed as a historic place.

Inside the chamber, Griffin-1 got very hot and very cold. It was heated to 75 degrees Celsius and cooled to minus 100 degrees Celsius. This tests the extreme temperatures the spacecraft will face. Engineers also used a crane to put the spacecraft inside the tall chamber.

After the tests, Griffin-1 was sent to a facility in Pittsburgh for final assembly. It is expected to launch in late 2026 on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket. The lander will carry more than 455 kilograms of cargo to the Moon.

passages.title: Antarctic Sea Ice in 2026
passages.content:
Antarctic sea ice grows and shrinks each year. It usually reaches its largest size in September. This is the end of winter in the Southern Hemisphere. In 2026, the ice reached its maximum on September 14. It covered about 17.59 million square kilometers. This was the third-lowest maximum in the satellite record.

The Antarctic is a large continent surrounded by ocean. So sea ice has more room to grow in winter. But the ice also reaches warmer areas, so more of it melts in summer. The ice usually shrinks to its smallest size in February. Scientists use satellites to measure the ice. Satellites can see the ice even through clouds.

passages.title: Tiny Brains and Plants in Space
passages.content:
NASA is sending science experiments to the International Space Station. One study sends very small, lab-grown models of the human brain to space for five weeks. Scientists compare these tiny brain models with the same kind kept on Earth. They want to learn how a short spaceflight affects the human brain. This may help protect astronauts on future trips to the Moon and beyond.

Another study looks at plants in space. It tests if plant diseases grow faster and worse in microgravity. Scientists compare plants grown on Earth with plants grown on the space station. The plants are infected with a disease-causing fungus. The results could help farmers on Earth grow stronger crops. Space crops also give astronauts food, oxygen, and clean water.

The mission also carries a small device to test astronaut health faster in space. A final study looks at antibiotic-resistant bacteria on the space station. Astronauts clean and test surfaces to watch these bacteria. This work may help keep astronauts safe from infections. The results may also help people on Earth understand superbugs.

passages.title: Testing Heat Shields by Taking Out the Trash
passages.content:
NASA is testing new heat shields for astronauts. The test uses trash. A cargo spacecraft left the International Space Station. It carried 12 small capsules. The capsules were made by students at the University of Kentucky. They held heat shield materials. The spacecraft was full of waste. Soon it will break apart in Earth's atmosphere. Then the capsules will fly out. They will collect data during re-entry. Small sensors measure heat, pressure, motion, and light. Satellites send the data to researchers. NASA scientist Keith Peterson said it is a smart way to get flight data on new materials.

The capsules test many kinds of heat shields. Some materials are old and proven. One is a 3D-printed heat shield. Others are new. One new material is more flexible, faster to make, and less expensive. This is important for future Mars missions. Mars has a thinner atmosphere, so spacecraft need less heat protection. One capsule is shaped like an umbrella. It can fold and make a bigger surface to slow the spacecraft. Another capsule tests a design for the Dragonfly mission to Titan, a moon of Saturn. This fast and low-cost test may help the next generation of space travel.

passages.content:
September is a rainy month in Thailand. Many towns get afternoon rain and storms. But in late September and early October 2026, very heavy rain would not stop. Low land in many parts of the country was soon under water.

NASA satellites took pictures of the same area in 2025 and in 2026. In the 2026 picture, dark blue floodwater covers a large area of farms and fish ponds beside the Bang Pakong River. The 2025 picture does not show this. The pictures use false colors so people can see water and plants more easily.

passages.title: When the Cotton Fields Turned Brown
passages.content:
In 2025, farmland around Lubbock, Texas, looked green. Satellite pictures showed healthy fields and lakes with water. One year later, in September 2026, the same area looked very different. The fields were brown and dry. Most of the small lakes had no water.

The 2026 drought hurt cotton farmers. One farmer said about 90 percent of her dryland cotton was dead. Some wells stopped working because there was not enough groundwater. Farmers in this region use water from underground to grow their crops. When the rain did come, it was not enough to end the drought.

passages.title: Arctic Sea Ice Reaches Its Low Point
passages.content:
A layer of frozen seawater covers the Arctic Ocean. This sea ice grows in the long, cold winter. It usually reaches its biggest size in March. Then it melts in summer. It reaches its smallest size in September. Satellites show that the ice is now smaller than it was many years ago.

In 2026, the sea ice reached its smallest size on September 12. It covered about 4.6 million square kilometers. This is the 10th-lowest size in the satellite record. The lowest size was in September 2012.

The ice is also thinner now. Thinner ice melts more easily. Winter ice is shrinking too. Scientists say natural changes and rising global temperatures work together to melt more ice. They think the Arctic could have almost no ice in summer at least once before the middle of the 21st century.

passages.title: The Moon's Spark Problem
passages.content:
Astronauts walk on the Moon near the South Pole. Walking makes electric charge build up on their spacesuits. The dark, shadowed areas make it worse. In these dark places, the charge cannot go away. So the astronaut becomes like a walking battery with a lot of charge.

When the astronaut comes back to the spacecraft, the spacecraft has a little positive charge in the sunlight. The astronaut has a big negative charge. When they touch, a spark can jump. This spark is called electrostatic discharge. The spark can hurt the suit, damage electronics, and shock the astronaut.

passages.title: Why Is the Water Brown?
passages.content:
In Canada, rivers flow into Hannah Bay and Rupert Bay. The water in these rivers often looks brown. The Cree people have a word for this color: pahtaaunaakun. It means "the color of singed beaver."

The brown color comes from dead leaves, roots, bark, and soil. These things break down in water and make it look like tea. The rivers carry this brown water into the bays. The water mixes with the blue water of James Bay.

Beavers are important in this area. The Cree people have hunted beaver for a very long time. In the 1660s, European traders came to Rupert Bay. They wanted beaver pelts. They started the Hudson's Bay Company. Beavers are also in Cree stories. One story is about a giant and a huge beaver.

passages.title: Moon-Like Rock in Madagascar
passages.content:
An astronaut on the International Space Station took a photo of Madagascar on August 28, 2026. The photo shows a bright, round rock area. This rock is called anorthosite. It is common on the Moon and looks light and shiny there. People can see it from Earth as the lunar highlands.

Anorthosite is also found on Earth. In southern Madagascar, it makes a round feature called the Saririaky massif. Scientists think this rock formed at least 600 million years ago. The rock around it shows that high heat and pressure changed it long ago. This happened when pieces of land now called Africa, India, Madagascar, Australia, and Antarctica crashed together. They formed a giant supercontinent named Gondwana.

Scientists study anorthosite on Earth to learn about the Moon. Moon rocks are more than 4 billion years old. Some anorthosite in Montana matches the Moon's rock very well.

passages.title: Perseverance Finds Light Rocks on Mars
passages.content:
NASA's Perseverance rover is on Mars. It spent six months exploring a place called "Lac de Charmes." This area is beyond the western rim of Jezero crater. The rover found many light-colored rocks there. Mars usually has dark rocks, so this was a surprise. The team wanted to know what these rocks are and how they got there.

Perseverance studied the rocks. Data shows that many of them are igneous rocks called gabbro. These rocks are rich in iron and magnesium. They usually form deep in the crust when magma cools slowly. So how did these deep rocks reach the surface? The rover is investigating a possible bedrock area between the light rocks and loose regolith. Early images suggest a breccia. A breccia is made of light and dark angular rock pieces. One idea is that the light rocks eroded out of this breccia. Breccias often form through violent processes, like asteroid impacts on early Mars. Maybe impacts dug up these light blocks. Only time will tell.

passages.content:
Heavy rain hit Nepal from September 24 to 27, 2026. The rain came late in the monsoon season. It caused landslides and made the Gandak River rise very high. The river is also called the Narayani. It reached record levels in Nepal and India.

NASA satellites took pictures of the river on September 20 and September 29, 2026. In the false-color pictures, water looks blue, plants look bright green, and clouds look light blue. On September 29, the river looked much wider. Water went over embankments and flooded farms and towns along the river. News reports said floods and landslides affected hundreds of villages and displaced thousands of people. A water gauge in Nepal reached 11.94 meters on September 27. passages.title: What to See in the October 2026 Night Sky
passages.content:
In October 2026, there are three things to see in the night sky. On October 4, Saturn is easy to see. Earth passes between the Sun and Saturn. So Saturn rises around sunset and stays visible for much of the night. On October 6, a thin crescent Moon appears close to bright Jupiter before sunrise.

The Orionid meteor shower peaks on the night of October 21 and the morning of October 22. These meteors come from tiny pieces of debris left by Halley's Comet. A bright Moon will make some faint meteors hard to see. Your best chance may be a few hours before dawn, after the Moon sets. Find a dark place, give your eyes time to adjust, and look up.

On the night of October 27, the Moon passes close to a famous star cluster called the Pleiades, also known as the Seven Sisters. Look east in the evening. The Pleiades look like a slightly fuzzy group of 6 to 7 stars. You can see them with your eyes, but binoculars or a telescope show more detail.

passages.title: An Island of Fields in a Wet Delta
passages.content:
The Saskatchewan River Delta is a very large inland delta in Canada. Most of it is too wet for farming. But inside this wet place, there is an "island" of fields. The fields have straight edges. They are west of the town of The Pas. This is Manitoba's northernmost farming area. It is called the Carrot River Valley.

Farmers in this valley grew mostly canola and spring wheat in 2025. In July 2026, many fields were green. Planting started later than in areas to the south because the ground was wet. In September, farmers had harvested some of the crops. Water is a big challenge here. In the 1950s, a flood control and drainage project began. Today, farming still needs dikes and pumps to protect fields from floods.

passages.title: A Cloud on Top of a Fire Cloud
passages.content:
In summer 2026, scientists flew over a fire in Montana. They studied fire clouds. A fire cloud is a tall cloud made by a wildfire. On August 11, they saw a special cloud on top of a fire cloud. It was a pileus cloud. Pileus means "cap" in Latin. The cap cloud was thin and smooth. It looked like a veil.

How did the cap cloud form? Hot air from the fire rose very fast. It pushed up a layer of moist air above it. The moist air rose and cooled. Its water vapor turned into a cloud. This is like air going over a mountain. But here, the fire cloud was the "mountain."

Cap clouds do not last long. They often stay for only a few minutes. Scientists took pictures about every 30 minutes. They saw the cap cloud in just one picture. The cap cloud shows that the air above the fire was moving very fast.

passages.title: Robots Helping Astronauts
passages.content:

The team is part of a larger group that also builds rovers for other planets. The team has 16 members. They work on two famous robots: Robonaut 2 and Valkyrie. passages.title: The Hidden Valleys Under Greenland's Ice
passages.content:
Greenland has a very big ice sheet. It covers 1.7 million square kilometers. In some places, the ice is more than 3 kilometers thick. Under all this ice, there are valleys. People cannot see them directly. Now, scientists have a new way to map them from space.

Ice moves over valleys and hills. This makes small bumps and dips on the ice surface. Satellites see these bumps and dips. Scientists use them to learn the shape of the land below. They mapped 1,943 valleys under the ice. About one third of these valleys are new to science.

Why does this matter? Ice flows faster in valleys. This can make the ice sheet change. Scientists say better maps may help us understand the ice sheet's future.

passages.content:
In autumn, you can see a special star called Algol. It is in the constellation Perseus. People also call it the 'Demon Star' or 'The Ghoul'. You can find it in the northeastern sky after 9 PM. Algol is not one star. It is a triple-star system. Two of the stars move around each other. Every three days, one star passes in front of the other. This makes Algol look dimmer for a short time. It goes from bright to a little dimmer. Then it gets bright again. This is like a blinking eye. You can compare Algol with a nearby star called Almach. Use binoculars or a small telescope. Algol and Almach have similar brightness. When Algol dims, you can see the change.

Another spooky thing is the Witch Head Nebula. It is between the constellations Eridanus and Orion. It is about 900 light-years away from Earth. It is a reflection nebula. It shines because of light from the star Rigel. You cannot see it with just your eyes. You need a very large telescope and dark skies. People can take pictures of it in a few hours.

passages.content:
NASA's Perseverance rover is exploring a place called "Lac de Charmes" on Mars. This area has valleys and ridges. The rocks there are very old. They formed when Mars was a young planet. Long ago, asteroids hit Mars. The rocks formed at that time. They are older than the rocks inside Jezero crater. The Jezero rocks formed later in rivers and lakes. The old rocks can teach us about early Mars.

The rover drove in a looping path. It made 13 abrasion patches on rocks. An abrasion patch is a small spot where the rover rubs a rock to see inside. Scientists found that many rocks formed from cooled lava or magma. Some rocks formed after a violent impact. The rover team also went to a place nicknamed "Idubi." There they saw hundreds of light-colored boulders. One boulder had a light-and-dark texture unlike any the rover had seen. The team tried to sample it, but the rock was too hard.

passages.title: Aluminum Alloy 2219: A Space Metal
passages.content:

Casting makes large metal shapes. But bad casting can cause small defects. These defects can make the metal weak. Then the metal may not work well. NASA recommends a homogenizing step after casting. After homogenization, the metal is forged and rolled. This makes the metal stronger. The metal has smaller grains and better properties. So, good steps make a strong metal for space.

passages.title: Hydrazine: A Space Fuel That Must Stay Warm
passages.content:
Hydrazine is a fuel used in some spacecraft. It freezes at about 1.6°C. When it freezes, it can shrink. Then, when it warms up, it can expand too much. This can break pipes and valves.

NASA has seen this problem before. Space Shuttle fuel lines could burst after freezing and thawing. Voyager spacecraft had to be kept warm to avoid blockages. Frozen hydrazine can also become slushy. Slush can block flow and cause engine problems. Leaks are dangerous because hydrazine is toxic.

So NASA keeps hydrazine warm with heaters and insulation. If freezing happens, the system must not be used until engineers check it. They thaw it slowly and evenly. They also test for damage. Keeping hydrazine above freezing is the best way to stay safe.

NASA and the State Department started the Artemis Accords in 2020 with seven other founding nations. The Artemis Accords are practical principles. They aim to improve transparency, safety, and coordination among nations as they explore the Moon, Mars, and beyond. Signing opens the door to future lunar exploration with NASA.

passages.title: NASA Looks at Health Risks in Space
passages.content:
NASA asked a group of experts to study health risks for astronauts. The group looked at problems like decompression sickness. This can happen when people work outside a spacecraft. They also studied blood clots and a heart feature called PFO.

The experts shared some ideas. They said a small PFO does not pose a big risk. They did not say all astronauts must be tested for a large PFO. But if a crew member has a large PFO, they should be told and offered a way to close it. The group also said more studies are needed.

NASA wants astronauts to stay safe during long missions to the Moon and beyond. The experts said rules and planning can help lower risks. They also said crews need clear guidance about some medicines, because these medicines may hide signs of sickness.

passages.title: Why Earth Has Seasons
passages.content:
Earth moves around the Sun. Earth also spins on a tilted axis. The tilt is about 23.5 degrees. This tilt causes the seasons. Imagine a spinning top leaning to one side.

In June, the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun. It gets more direct sunlight and longer days. So June is summer in the Northern Hemisphere. In December, the Southern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun. So December is summer there.

March and September are equinoxes. They are the middle points between the two extremes. On these days, day and night are nearly equal in length. NASA's EPIC camera takes pictures of Earth from space. These pictures show how Earth's tilt changes what we see during the year.

passages.title: Arctic Ice and the Longer Melt Season
passages.content:
Arctic sea ice melts in spring and freezes in fall. Since 1979, satellites have watched this. The melt season is now about 40 days longer than in 1979. Most of this change happened before 2010. Since 2010, the season has been about the same, but it still changes a lot from year to year. The later freeze in fall caused most of the longer season, not an earlier melt in spring.

In the 2000s, thin ice melted. Dark ocean water opened up. The water took in more sunlight. This extra heat made the ice freeze later. Since 2010, more clouds have blocked some sunlight. So the season stopped getting longer. But the Arctic still warms very fast, and the ice is still thin.

Scientists are not sure if this stop will last. The Arctic may soon have another time of fast ice loss. Satellites will keep watching the ice.

passages.title: What Is an Equinox?
passages.content:
An equinox happens twice every year, in March and September. The word comes from Latin and means "equal night." On the day of an equinox, the Sun shines equally on the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. This is the only time when both the North Pole and the South Pole get sunlight at the same time.

The equinox marks the exact moment when the center of the Sun crosses the plane of Earth's equator. After the March equinox, people see the Sun's path move further north each day until the June solstice. Then it moves south. After the September equinox, the Sun keeps moving south until the December solstice.

The length of day and night is not exactly equal on the equinox. The Sun is a sphere, not a point, and our atmosphere bends its light. This adds a few minutes of light to every day. So day and night are very close to equal, but not perfect.

passages.title: A Pulsar Catches a Star's Wind
passages.content:
Astronomers used a space telescope called XRISM to study two stars far away. One star is very big and hot. Gas moves away from it all the time. People call this moving gas a stellar wind.

The other star is small and heavy. It is called a pulsar. The pulsar moves around the big star. When the pulsar passes through the wind, it catches some gas. The gas moves toward the pulsar very fast. Then the gas gets hot and makes strong X-ray light. These bright X-ray flares can last for several days.

The telescope watched the two stars for about 16 hours. It saw that the gas was moving toward the pulsar at about 540,000 kilometers per hour. This was the first clear view of a star's wind falling onto a small, heavy star.

passages.title: Earth's Moving Center
passages.content:
Earth's water moves between land and oceans. This moves Earth's center of mass. It moves only a little, by fractions of an inch. NASA scientists study this with satellites. Earth's center of mass is important for satellite navigation and for measuring height.

Water, ice, and air sit on Earth and change with the seasons. In spring, snow melts. Oceans move. Dense winter air pushes down. These things change Earth's surface load. So Earth's center of mass moves around its geometric center. It can move by several millimeters.

Scientists use satellites to track this movement. Satellites orbit Earth's center of mass. Small changes in distance between satellites and ground stations show the movement. A new NASA-led technique is more accurate. It uses GPS tracking and data from low Earth orbit satellites. It also considers how water and ice change Earth's crust.

passages.title: The Youngest Known Planet
passages.content:
Astronomers have found the youngest known planet. It is called Elias 2-24 b. It is less than one million years old. The planet is still growing in a disk of dust and gas around its star. The star is about 450 light-years from Earth. The planet is about as big as Jupiter.

Planets outside our solar system are called exoplanets. Most exoplanets we know are billions of years old. They are hard to see when they are young because dust covers them. Astronomers used a special tool to block the star's light. Then they found the baby planet in a gap in the disk.

This discovery helps scientists learn how planets form. It shows that planets may form faster than we thought. Studying this young planet is like a time machine. It helps us imagine what our own solar system was like long ago.

passages.title: Purple Light in the Sky
passages.content:
An astronaut on the International Space Station took photos of the aurora on September 7, 2026. The aurora filled Earth's atmosphere with green, red, and purple light. The astronaut, Jessica Meir, posted about the "brilliant purple" light on September 8. She said it made her want to "kiss the sky."

Auroras start when the Sun sends charged particles toward Earth. These particles move into Earth's upper atmosphere. There, they excite nitrogen and oxygen atoms. The atoms then release light. The color of the light depends on the gas and its altitude. Oxygen can make green and red. Nitrogen can glow blue or pink. Sometimes the colors seem to mix, so the aurora looks purple, pink, or even white.

passages.title: Curiosity on Mars: Studying Wind-Blown Sand
passages.content:
NASA's Curiosity rover is on Mars. It studies the planet and sends facts back to Earth. This week, the team planned new work for the rover. The rover used its arm on Sols 5003 and 5004. A sol is one day on Mars. The arm looked at a long, narrow ripple of sand called Chocolatal. Wind made this ripple.

The team also used the rover's camera to take special pictures. They wanted to see the side of the sand ripple. The camera can look at the surface from the side, like a dog close to the ground. The team looked for layers in the sand. Later, the rover will study an interesting gray stone. The stone sits on bedrock with large nodules. The rover will also take pictures of the Chocolatal area again.

passages.title: Look Up at the Moon with NASA
passages.content:
International Observe the Moon Night is a yearly event. It brings people together to learn about the Moon. The program began in 2010. People around the world join by looking at the Moon, doing activities, making art, and more. This year, the event is on Sept. 19.

At NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, there is a special celebration. It runs from 6 p.m. to 9 p.m. Visitors can do hands-on activities and make crafts. They can also take selfies. Outside, there are telescopes. If the weather is good, people can look at the Moon and other objects up close. Inside, guests can see a real Moon rock from Apollo 14.

The event is free and fun for families. You do not need to register, but registering early helps the team plan. The event happens rain or shine. People who cannot travel can join from anywhere in the world by looking at the Moon with friends and family or joining a virtual event.

passages.title: Summer Training for Future Astronauts
passages.content:
NASA has 10 new astronaut candidates. They started training in 2025. They are about halfway through a program that takes almost two years. This training prepares them for missions to low Earth orbit, the Moon, and Mars.

In May, the candidates studied rocks in a classroom. Then they went to New Mexico to practice in the field. They hiked and studied rocks there. Some candidates also trained in Iceland. They learned to observe rocks, use tools, find their way, and work as a team. These skills will help on future Artemis missions to the Moon.

The candidates also learned to fly airplanes. They flew NASA's WB-57 plane and began flying the T-38 jet. They practiced in a special altitude chamber, too. This helps them get ready for high-altitude flights and space. They also did water survival training. They will finish training in 2027.

passages.title: Fall Colors Come Early in Northern Canada
passages.content: Fall comes early in far northern Canada. In Nunavut, the tundra plants start to change color in early September. They turn red, orange, and yellow. The area has willow and birch shrubs, blueberries, and bearberries. NASA used satellite images to see the change. One image from July 27 shows green plants. Another image from September 6 shows fall colors. A NASA study looked at seven years of satellite data. It found that this area changes color earlier than most places in North America. The peak color time is short there. Sometimes it lasts only a week or less. In fall, leaves lose chlorophyll. Chlorophyll is the green stuff in leaves. It needs sunlight and warm weather. When days get shorter and colder, chlorophyll goes down. Then other colors show: yellow and red. Citizen scientists can help NASA track fall color. They watch and record leaf colors in spring and fall.

passages.title: Plants and Health in Space
passages.content:
NASA chose 12 new studies to help people in space. Six studies are about food. NASA wants to grow plants in space. Plants can help people live on the Moon and Mars. Some studies look at how plants grow in space. One study looks at resurrection plants. These plants can live in very dry places. Another study looks at algae. Algae are tiny plants. They can help in space life-support systems.

Six other studies are about health. Space can change the human body. One study looks at lunar dust. Lunar dust may affect breathing and the immune system. Another study looks for drugs. These drugs may help people stay healthy in space. Other studies look at radiation and aging. The studies may help find health problems early.

Scientists from 10 institutions in 8 states do these studies. This work can help astronauts go farther and stay longer in space.
